content_html:
A README file in your ~/Downloads folder should not be able to expose your SSH keys. A calendar invite should not be able to trigger actions in your smart home. An email should not be able to persuade an AI assistant to leak your company's files.

Yet researchers have demonstrated attacks against agents connected to local files, calendars, mailboxes, browsers, and external tools — and vendors have disclosed and patched real vulnerabilities in shipping AI products. The evidence ranges from controlled lab demonstrations to fixed production CVEs. It is not a record of widespread in-the-wild compromise, and this guide is careful to say which is which.

The shared risk underneath almost all of it is indirect prompt injection: an agent reads content someone else controls and treats part of that content as instructions. The result can be an unauthorized tool call, data exposure, or an action you never intended.

This is a field guide to that problem across Claude, GPT, Gemini, Copilot, Cursor, and the open-model ecosystem. It maps the real, named attacks, explains the one idea that ties most of them together, separates true prompt injection from the adjacent risks it gets lumped with, and lays out what actually helps.

No working exploit code is included here. Every example is based on public research or a disclosed vulnerability, and payloads are illustrative, not operational.

1. The one idea behind most of these attacks

Security researcher Simon Willison coined the phrase that explains a lot of what follows: the lethal trifecta. It's a useful way to assess agent risk, built from three ingredients:

Ingredient What it means Example
🔑 Access to private data The agent can read things you don't want leaked Your repo, email, Drive, SSH keys
📥 Exposure to untrusted content It ingests text/images someone else wrote A web page, a GitHub issue, a PDF, a calendar invite
📤 A way to send data out It can cause an outbound effect Render an image, open a URL, call a tool, write a file

The combination makes data theft particularly plausible: untrusted content supplies the instruction, private data is the prize, and the outbound channel carries it away. It is not a guarantee that a system with only one or two ingredients is safe — an agent can still be manipulated into modifying a file, deleting data, or taking an unwanted action without all three. But when all three line up, a single sentence of attacker text is often enough.

Almost every "new" AI vulnerability below is really the same trifecta reassembled from different parts.

The deeper reason it's so hard: messages, roles, and formatting give an LLM structure, but that structure is not a dependable security boundary between your trusted instructions and attacker-controlled content. Untrusted documents and tool results can still steer the model's reasoning and its tool choices. The application has to enforce authority, permissions, and action limits outside the model — the model alone can't be trusted to hold the line.

2. How an indirect prompt injection actually works

Most of these attacks are indirect: the attacker never talks to your agent. They plant text somewhere your agent will later read it, and wait.

To a human reviewer this is a comment. To an agent with file access and commit rights, it reads as a to-do list. Nothing is "hacked" in the traditional sense — the model did what the text asked.

3. Three different problem classes (read this first)

This is where a lot of coverage gets sloppy, so let's be precise. Not everything that can compromise an agent system is prompt injection. There are three distinct classes here, with different causes and different fixes:

Problem class Examples in this guide What's actually happening
Prompt injection / instruction confusion Malicious READMEs, MCP tool poisoning, Unicode/ANSI smuggling, EchoLeak, AgentFlayer, Gemini calendar, Comet, image injection, Morris II Attacker-controlled content influences the agent's plans, decisions, or tool calls
Implementation vulnerabilities CVE-2025-6514 in mcp-remote A conventional software bug in agent infrastructure — it doesn't depend on the model obeying anything
AI/ML supply-chain compromise Malicious pickle files, malicious loader scripts, namespace reuse, slopsquatting The model, package, or artifact you load/install is itself attacker-controlled

They belong in the same security review because all three can compromise systems built around AI agents — but conflating them leads to the wrong defenses. The catalog below flags which class each item belongs to.

4. The attack catalog

A. File & repo based · prompt injection

The attacker puts the payload in a file your coding agent will read.

  • Malicious Markdown / README / AGENTS.md — hidden instructions in a .md file (often in a repo or ~/Downloads) get read by Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor and executed as instructions. The vector most people met first.
  • Rules File Backdoor (Pillar Security, Mar 2025) — the payload hides in a tool's config (.cursor/rules, Copilot instruction files) using zero-width and bidirectional Unicode characters, invisible in the normal GitHub review UI. Both vendors initially treated it as the user's responsibility; GitHub later added a warning when hidden Unicode is detected in file contents. Pillar reported that the payload could persist across forks.
  • Ghostcommit (OffSeq, 2026) — an instruction hidden inside an image tells a coding agent to read .env and smuggle the secrets into code as numeric constants, evading secret scanners because AI reviewers don't inspect image files. (2026 research demonstration.)

🎯 Targets: Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Codex — any agent that reads project files as context.

B. The MCP tool layer · mostly prompt injection

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets agents use external tools. The tools — and their descriptions — are themselves untrusted content.

  • Tool Poisoning (Invariant Labs, Apr 2025) — malicious instructions hidden in a tool's description/metadata, which may not be visible in the client's normal tool presentation but the model reads and obeys. The proof-of-concept made Cursor read ~/.ssh/id_rsa. Now codified as OWASP MCP03:2025.
  • Rug pull — a tool is benign at install, then swaps in malicious behavior in a later update.
  • Tool shadowing — one malicious server redefines or intercepts a trusted server's tool.
  • GitHub MCP exploit (Milanta & Beurer-Kellner, May 2025) — an attacker files a malicious GitHub issue in a public repo; when the agent reads issues, the hidden instruction makes it leak private-repo names into a public pull request. A textbook lethal trifecta.
MCP attack Where the payload lives Classic outcome
Tool poisoning Tool description Reads secrets / runs commands
Rug pull A later tool update Delayed compromise
Tool shadowing A competing server Hijacks a trusted tool
Malicious data (e.g. GitHub issue) Content a tool returns Private-data exfiltration

⚠️ Not prompt injection — an implementation bug: CVE-2025-6514 is an OS command-injection flaw in the mcp-remote OAuth proxy (versions 0.0.5–0.1.15, fixed in 0.1.16, CVSS 9.6). A malicious MCP server a user connects to can run commands on their machine. It's a serious MCP-ecosystem risk, but it has nothing to do with a model obeying a prompt. One academic study reported tool-poisoning indicators in ~5.5% of the open-source MCP servers it sampled — that's a research finding on one sample, not proof that 5.5% of all public servers are exploitable.

C. Invisible text: Unicode, emoji & ANSI smuggling · delivery mechanism

Not an attack on its own — a way to make the instruction invisible to humans while machines still read it.

  • ASCII / Unicode-Tag smuggling — characters in the Unicode Tags block (mainly U+E0020–U+E007E, which mirror printable ASCII) render blank in most contexts but remain readable to the model. Rides in docs, support tickets, web pages, and RAG inputs. Visibility depends on the app. (SecureLayer7, Promptfoo)
  • Emoji smuggling (FireTail, Jan 2026) — instructions hidden inside emoji via variation selectors. In the reported test, the model did not decode them automatically; the researchers had to prompt it to inspect and translate the hidden content. Treat it as a demonstrated technique under specific conditions, not a universal capability.
  • ANSI terminal escape codes (Trail of Bits, Apr 2025) — escape sequences make text invisible in a terminal while the bytes an agent's tool wrapper captures stay intact. Demonstrated against Claude Code; any CLI agent that doesn't strip escapes is exposed.

🧪 Why it's nasty: these characters can sail through human code review and the PR UI — the payload is right there in the diff, you just can't see it.

D. Zero-click via email, calendar & connectors · prompt injection

The scariest class: no click, no download, no action from the victim. The content arrives in a channel the agent automatically ingests.

  • EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711, Aim Labs) — a crafted email sits in the mailbox; when the user later asks Copilot an unrelated question, the email is RAG-pulled into context and exfiltrates SharePoint content, chat history, and files via an auto-fetched Markdown image. Microsoft rated it critical (CVSS 9.3; some trackers score it lower), named the class "LLM Scope Violation," patched it before public disclosure, and reported no known exploitation in the wild.
  • ShadowLeak (Radware) — a service-side injection against ChatGPT's Deep Research agent that exfiltrates Gmail/Drive/Outlook data entirely inside OpenAI's infrastructure, so client-side defenses never see it. Reported to OpenAI in June 2025, fixed by early August, publicly disclosed September 18, 2025.
  • AgentFlayer (Zenity Labs, Aug 2025) — zero-click against ChatGPT Connectors. The demonstrated case hid a prompt in a shared document as nearly invisible white text in a tiny font, told ChatGPT to pull Google Drive secrets, and exfiltrated them through a Markdown image URL. When OpenAI blocked arbitrary image servers, the researchers routed the image through trusted Azure Blob storage. The ChatGPT case was patched; the researchers note other connector targets were flagged "won't fix."
  • "Invitation Is All You Need" (Black Hat, Aug 2025) — promptware hidden in a Google Calendar invite hijacks Gemini when it summarizes your week. Across 14 attack scenarios, researchers rated 73% of the assessed threats high- or critical-risk, including controlled demos of opening smart-home windows and starting calls. Google deployed mitigations. These were controlled research demonstrations, not a real-world campaign in anyone's home.

E. Browser agents · prompt injection

An AI browser reads every page you visit — including the attacker's. Two separate pieces of research, with different status:

  • Comet page-injection (Brave, Aug 2025) — hidden instructions on a web page executed by the agent as commands, later extended to text hidden in an image. Perplexity shipped initial fixes, but Brave's follow-up testing found the mitigation incomplete. (Simon Willison)
  • CometJacking (LayerX) — a separate crafted-URL attack: opening the link makes the browser's AI run hidden instructions and exfiltrate data. Opening the URL requires user interaction, so this is not zero-click. Per the disclosure, Perplexity marked the report "Not Applicable," and no fix is confirmed in the cited material.

🌐 Browser agents assemble the full trifecta by default: your logged-in sessions, arbitrary web pages, and navigation. Handle with care.

F. Multimodal & image injection · prompt injection

If the model can read images, the image can carry the payload.

  • Off-white text / "blank" images (Goodside & Rehberger, 2023 →) — subtle text in an apparently blank image can override or bias the model's response. Separately, Rehberger demonstrated an image-borne payload that pushed a model to leak conversation context — exfiltration is a distinct outcome shown in that specific demo. (Simon Willison)
  • Adversarial / visual prompt injection on web agents (2025 research — e.g. VPI-Bench, WebInject) — perturbations and rendered text steer screenshot-driven agents into the wrong action. These are benchmark/lab findings, not disclosed product CVEs.

G. Supply chain: poisoned models & packages · supply-chain compromise

The compromise ships before any prompt is written. Three distinct incidents often wrongly bundled together:

  • 2024 — ~100 malicious models (JFrog / The Hacker News): pickle-based model files that run arbitrary shell on torch.load().
  • 2025 — PickleScan evasion (PointGuard AI): the nullifAI technique packed malformed pickle files in 7z to slip past Hugging Face's scanner; HF then updated PickleScan.
  • 2026 — fake "OpenAI" repository (InfoWorld): used a malicious loader.py to fetch and run an infostealer (not a torch.load() pickle attack). Reported at 200,000+ downloads (some coverage says 244,000) — but downloads are not confirmed infections, so read that number as reach, not victims.
  • Slopsquatting vs typosquatting — slopsquatting registers package names an LLM hallucinated in generated code; typosquatting mimics real names. A study found hallucinated package names in both commercial and open-source model output. An agent doesn't always auto-install them — but a confident wrong name is a pre-seeded foothold.

🧷 Prefer safetensors over pickle. It removes the unsafe-deserialization risk — but it does not make a malicious repo, loader script, or surrounding package safe.

H. Self-propagating worms · prompt injection, weaponized

  • Morris II (Cohen, Bitton & Nassi, Mar 2024) — the first self-replicating GenAI worm. An adversarial self-replicating prompt lives in a RAG store, performs a malicious action in each app it reaches (spam, data exfiltration), and spreads to the next. Demonstrated against GPT-4, Gemini Pro, and LLaVA in a controlled lab — not released in the wild, but proof that injection + RAG persistence = propagation.

7. Why this is genuinely hard to fix

  • Structure isn't a security boundary. Message roles and formatting exist, but they don't reliably separate trusted instructions from attacker-controlled content. The model infers what to obey from meaning — and meaning is what an attacker controls.
  • Filtering is whack-a-mole. Strip Unicode tag characters and attackers move to emoji variation selectors or rewording. A classifier that catches the obvious attack often misses the reworded one.
  • The capability is the vulnerability. The whole point of an agent is to read untrusted content and take actions. Remove either and you've removed the product.
  • The durable fixes live outside the model — provenance, least privilege, and egress control, enforced whether or not the text fooled the model.

8. What actually helps

No single control solves prompt injection. Defense-in-depth measurably shrinks the blast radius.

Layer What it does Caveat
Break the trifecta Don't give one agent unrestricted private data + untrusted content + outbound actions together The single highest-leverage move
Input sanitization Visualize/escape suspicious characters (Unicode tags, zero-width, ANSI), normalize Does not solve injection — attackers reword or re-encode
Provenance / taint tracking Track where each value came from; treat tool/web output as untrusted Needs enforcement at the action boundary
Least privilege + human-in-the-loop Scope credentials; review sensitive actions Approval only works if the reviewer sees the real action and its arguments
Controlled egress A narrow egress broker, restrict auto-fetching of external images/URLs A broad cloud-domain allowlist is abusable — AgentFlayer used trusted Azure Blob
Output scanning Flag secrets / exfil patterns in output One layer only — data can leave via tool calls, URLs, or images without appearing in the visible reply
Supply-chain hygiene Prefer safetensors; scan models; pin & verify packages safetensors fixes deserialization, not a malicious repo/loader
Secure logging Log raw input to catch hidden code points Redact/escape — raw logs can themselves become a secret store

The highest-leverage idea is the first one, stated carefully:

Avoid giving a single agent unrestricted access to private data, arbitrary untrusted content, and unrestricted outbound actions at once. Where those capabilities are all needed, enforce scoped credentials, tool-level authorization, reviewed sensitive actions, and controlled egress — outside the model.

Design so that when (not if) a hidden instruction gets through, it hits a wall: no private data in reach, or no channel out, or no standing permission to act.

9. A 10-minute checklist

  • [ ] Visualize/escape invisible characters (Unicode tags, zero-width, ANSI) in anything an agent ingests — and treat all external content as untrusted.
  • [ ] Turn off "always allow." Require approval before an agent reads private repos, sends email, moves money, or deletes — and make the prompt show the real destination/arguments.
  • [ ] Use a narrow egress policy — restrict outbound URLs and auto-fetched image hosts; don't trust broad cloud domains wholesale.
  • [ ] Audit your MCP servers — pin versions (update mcp-remote ≥ 0.1.16), read tool descriptions, drop ones you can't vouch for.
  • [ ] Separate the trifecta — don't let one agent session hold private data and untrusted content and an exfil path.
  • [ ] Prefer safetensors; scan models; verify repositories and loader scripts, not just weights.
  • [ ] Log raw input securely (redacted, access-controlled) so hidden code points are reviewable without creating a secret store.
  • [ ] Treat tool and web output as untrusted by default — it's data, never instructions.

10. The takeaway

The markdown-file trick that's been making the rounds isn't a one-off — it's one entry in a fast-growing catalog spanning files, tools, invisible text, email, calendars, browsers, images, model weights, and self-replicating worms. The true prompt-injection cases all rhyme because they exploit the same thing: an AI agent can't reliably tell the content it reads from the commands it's given. The rest — implementation bugs and supply-chain compromises — ride in the same systems but need their own fixes.

You don't solve injection with a cleverer prompt. You contain it by designing so that a hidden instruction, when it lands, has nowhere to go. Break the trifecta, enforce authority outside the model, and most of this guide becomes a list of attacks with no payoff.

If this was useful, follow me — I write about AI security and the gap between "the demo worked" and "it survived contact with an attacker." Next up: a hands-on look at defending the tool-call boundary.

Your turn: what's the sneakiest AI-agent injection you've actually seen in the wild — or successfully defended against? Drop it in the comments. 👇

In the reported test, the model did not decode them automatically; the researchers had to prompt it to inspect and translate the hidden content. Treat it as a demonstrated technique under specific conditions, not a universal capability. ANSI terminal escape codes (Trail of Bits, Apr 2025) — escape sequences make text invisible in a terminal while the bytes an agent's tool wrapper captures stay intact. Demonstrated against Claude Code; any CLI agent that doesn't strip escapes is exposed. 🧪 Why it's nasty: these characters can sail through human code review and the PR UI — the payload is right there in the diff, you just can't see it. D. Zero-click via email, calendar & connectors · prompt injection The scariest class: no click, no download, no action from the victim. The content arrives in a channel the agent automatically ingests. EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711, Aim Labs) — a crafted email sits in the mailbox; when the user later asks Copilot an unrelated question, the email is RAG-pulled into context and exfiltrates SharePoint content, chat history, and files via an auto-fetched Markdown image. Microsoft rated it critical (CVSS 9.3; some trackers score it lower), named the class "LLM Scope Violation," patched it before public disclosure, and reported no known exploitation in the wild. ShadowLeak (Radware) — a service-side injection against ChatGPT's Deep Research agent that exfiltrates Gmail/Drive/Outlook data entirely inside OpenAI's infrastructure, so client-side defenses never see it. Reported to OpenAI in June 2025, fixed by early August, publicly disclosed September 18, 2025. AgentFlayer (Zenity Labs, Aug 2025) — zero-click against ChatGPT Connectors. The demonstrated case hid a prompt in a shared document as nearly invisible white text in a tiny font, told ChatGPT to pull Google Drive secrets, and exfiltrated them through a Markdown image URL. When OpenAI blocked arbitrary image servers, the researchers routed the image through trusted Azure Blob storage. The ChatGPT case was patched; the researchers note other connector targets were flagged "won't fix." "Invitation Is All You Need" (Black Hat, Aug 2025) — promptware hidden in a Google Calendar invite hijacks Gemini when it summarizes your week. Across 14 attack scenarios, researchers rated 73% of the assessed threats high- or critical-risk, including controlled demos of opening smart-home windows and starting calls. Google deployed mitigations. These were controlled research demonstrations, not a real-world campaign in anyone's home. E. Browser agents · prompt injection An AI browser reads every page you visit — including the attacker's. Two separate pieces of research, with different status: Comet page-injection (Brave, Aug 2025) — hidden instructions on a web page executed by the agent as commands, later extended to text hidden in an image. Perplexity shipped initial fixes, but Brave's follow-up testing found the mitigation incomplete. (Simon Willison) CometJacking (LayerX) — a separate crafted-URL attack: opening the link makes the browser's AI run hidden instructions and exfiltrate data. Opening the URL requires user interaction, so this is not zero-click. Per the disclosure, Perplexity marked the report "Not Applicable," and no fix is confirmed in the cited material. 🌐 Browser agents assemble the full trifecta by default: your logged-in sessions, arbitrary web pages, and navigation. Handle with care. F. Multimodal & image injection · prompt injection If the model can read images, the image can carry the payload. Off-white text / "blank" images (Goodside & Rehberger, 2023 →) — subtle text in an apparently blank image can override or bias the model's response. Separately, Rehberger demonstrated an image-borne payload that pushed a model to leak conversation context — exfiltration is a distinct outcome shown in that specific demo. (Simon Willison) Adversarial / visual prompt injection on web agents (2025 research — e.g. VPI-Bench, WebInject) — perturbations and rendered text steer screenshot-driven agents into the wrong action. These are benchmark/lab findings, not disclosed product CVEs. G. Supply chain: poisoned models & packages · supply-chain compromise The compromise ships before any prompt is written. Three distinct incidents often wrongly bundled together: 2024 — ~100 malicious models (JFrog / The Hacker News): pickle-based model files that run arbitrary shell on torch.load(). 2025 — PickleScan evasion (PointGuard AI): the nullifAI technique packed malformed pickle files in 7z to slip past Hugging Face's scanner; HF then updated PickleScan. 2026 — fake "OpenAI" repository (InfoWorld): used a malicious loader.py to fetch and run an infostealer (not a torch.load() pickle attack). Reported at 200,000+ downloads (some coverage says 244,000) — but downloads are not confirmed infections, so read that number as reach, not victims. Slopsquatting vs typosquatting — slopsquatting registers package names an LLM hallucinated in generated code; typosquatting mimics real names. A study found hallucinated package names in both commercial and open-source model output. An agent doesn't always auto-install them — but a confident wrong name is a pre-seeded foothold. 🧷 Prefer safetensors over pickle. It removes the unsafe-deserialization risk — but it does not make a malicious repo, loader script, or surrounding package safe. H. Self-propagating worms · prompt injection, weaponized Morris II (Cohen, Bitton & Nassi, Mar 2024) — the first self-replicating GenAI worm. An adversarial self-replicating prompt lives in a RAG store, performs a malicious action in each app it reaches (spam, data exfiltration), and spreads to the next. Demonstrated against GPT-4, Gemini Pro, and LLaVA in a controlled lab — not released in the wild, but proof that injection + RAG persistence = propagation. 5. That's significant without implying widespread real-world compromise. 7. Why this is genuinely hard to fix Structure isn't a security boundary. Message roles and formatting exist, but they don't reliably separate trusted instructions from attacker-controlled content. The model infers what to obey from meaning — and meaning is what an attacker controls. Filtering is whack-a-mole. Strip Unicode tag characters and attackers move to emoji variation selectors or rewording. A classifier that catches the obvious attack often misses the reworded one. The capability is the vulnerability. The whole point of an agent is to read untrusted content and take actions. Remove either and you've removed the product. The durable fixes live outside the model — provenance, least privilege, and egress control, enforced whether or not the text fooled the model. 8. What actually helps No single control solves prompt injection. Defense-in-depth measurably shrinks the blast radius. Layer What it does Caveat Break the trifecta Don't give one agent unrestricted private data + untrusted content + outbound actions together The single highest-leverage move Input sanitization Visualize/escape suspicious characters (Unicode tags, zero-width, ANSI), normalize Does not solve injection — attackers reword or re-encode Provenance / taint tracking Track where each value came from; treat tool/web output as untrusted Needs enforcement at the action boundary Least privilege + human-in-the-loop Scope credentials; review sensitive actions Approval only works if the reviewer sees the real action and its arguments Controlled egress A narrow egress broker, restrict auto-fetching of external images/URLs A broad cloud-domain allowlist is abusable — AgentFlayer used trusted Azure Blob Output scanning Flag secrets / exfil patterns in output One layer only — data can leave via tool calls, URLs, or images without appearing in the visible reply Supply-chain hygiene Prefer safetensors; scan models; pin & verify packages safetensors fixes deserialization, not a malicious repo/loader Secure logging Log raw input to catch hidden code points Redact/escape — raw logs can themselves become a secret store The highest-leverage idea is the first one, stated carefully: Avoid giving a single agent unrestricted access to private data, arbitrary untrusted content, and unrestricted outbound actions at once. Where those capabilities are all needed, enforce scoped credentials, tool-level authorization, reviewed sensitive actions, and controlled egress — outside the model. Design so that when (not if) a hidden instruction gets through, it hits a wall: no private data in reach, or no channel out, or no standing permission to act. 9. A 10-minute checklist [ ] Visualize/escape invisible characters (Unicode tags, zero-width, ANSI) in anything an agent ingests — and treat all external content as untrusted. [ ] Turn off "always allow." Require approval before an agent reads private repos, sends email, moves money, or deletes — and make the prompt show the real destination/arguments. [ ] Use a narrow egress policy — restrict outbound URLs and auto-fetched image hosts; don't trust broad cloud domains wholesale. [ ] Audit your MCP servers — pin versions (update mcp-remote ≥ 0.1.16), read tool descriptions, drop ones you can't vouch for. [ ] Separate the trifecta — don't let one agent session hold private data and untrusted content and an exfil path. [ ] Prefer safetensors; scan models; verify repositories and loader scripts, not just weights. [ ] Log raw input securely (redacted, access-controlled) so hidden code points are reviewable without creating a secret store. [ ] Treat tool and web output as untrusted by default — it's data, never instructions. 10. The takeaway The markdown-file trick that's been making the rounds isn't a one-off — it's one entry in a fast-growing catalog spanning files, tools, invisible text, email, calendars, browsers, images, model weights, and self-replicating worms. The true prompt-injection cases all rhyme because they exploit the same thing: an AI agent can't reliably tell the content it reads from the commands it's given. The rest — implementation bugs and supply-chain compromises — ride in the same systems but need their own fixes. You don't solve injection with a cleverer prompt. You contain it by designing so that a hidden instruction, when it lands, has nowhere to go. Break the trifecta, enforce authority outside the model, and most of this guide becomes a list of attacks with no payoff. If this was useful, follow me — I write about AI security and the gap between "the demo worked" and "it survived contact with an attacker." content_html_zh:
A README file in your ~/Downloads folder should not be able to expose your SSH keys. A calendar invite should not be able to trigger actions in your smart home. An email should not be able to persuade an AI assistant to leak your company's files.

Yet researchers have demonstrated attacks against agents connected to local files, calendars, mailboxes, browsers, and external tools — and vendors have disclosed and patched real vulnerabilities in shipping AI products. The evidence ranges from controlled lab demonstrations to fixed production CVEs. It is not a record of widespread in-the-wild compromise, and this guide is careful to say which is which.

The shared risk underneath almost all of it is indirect prompt injection: an agent reads content someone else controls and treats part of that content as instructions. The result can be an unauthorized tool call, data exposure, or an action you never intended.

This is a field guide to that problem across Claude, GPT, Gemini, Copilot, Cursor, and the open-model ecosystem. It maps the real, named attacks, explains the one idea that ties most of them together, separates true prompt injection from the adjacent risks it gets lumped with, and lays out what actually helps.

No working exploit code is included here. Every example is based on public research or a disclosed vulnerability, and payloads are illustrative, not operational.

1. The one idea behind most of these attacks

Security researcher Simon Willison coined the phrase that explains a lot of what follows: the lethal trifecta. It's a useful way to assess agent risk, built from three ingredients:

Ingredient 这意味着什么 例子
🔑 Access to private data The agent can read things you don't want leaked Your repo, email, Drive, SSH keys
📥 Exposure to untrusted content It ingests text/images someone else wrote A web page, a GitHub issue, a PDF, a calendar invite
📤 A way to send data out It can cause an outbound effect Render an image, open a URL, call a tool, write a file

The combination makes data theft particularly plausible: untrusted content supplies the instruction, private data is the prize, and the outbound channel carries it away. It is not a guarantee that a system with only one or two ingredients is safe — an agent can still be manipulated into modifying a file, deleting data, or taking an unwanted action without all three. But when all three line up, a single sentence of attacker text is often enough.

Almost every "new" AI vulnerability below is really the same trifecta reassembled from different parts.

The deeper reason it's so hard: messages, roles, and formatting give an LLM structure, but that structure is not a dependable security boundary between your trusted instructions and attacker-controlled content. Untrusted documents and tool results can still steer the model's reasoning and its tool choices. The application has to enforce authority, permissions, and action limits outside the model — the model alone can't be trusted to hold the line.

2. How an indirect prompt injection actually works

Most of these attacks are indirect: the attacker never talks to your agent. They plant text somewhere your agent will later read it, and wait.

To a human reviewer this is a comment. To an agent with file access and commit rights, it reads as a to-do list. Nothing is "hacked" in the traditional sense — the model did what the text asked.

3. Three different problem classes (read this first)

This is where a lot of coverage gets sloppy, so let's be precise. Not everything that can compromise an agent system is prompt injection. There are three distinct classes here, with different causes and different fixes:

Problem class Examples in this guide What's actually happening
Prompt injection / instruction confusion Malicious READMEs, MCP tool poisoning, Unicode/ANSI smuggling, EchoLeak, AgentFlayer, Gemini calendar, Comet, image injection, Morris II Attacker-controlled content influences the agent's plans, decisions, or tool calls
Implementation vulnerabilities CVE-2025-6514 in mcp-remote A conventional software bug in agent infrastructure — it doesn't depend on the model obeying anything
AI/ML supply-chain compromise Malicious pickle files, malicious loader scripts, namespace reuse, slopsquatting The model, package, or artifact you load/install is itself attacker-controlled

They belong in the same security review because all three can compromise systems built around AI agents — but conflating them leads to the wrong defenses. The catalog below flags which class each item belongs to.

4. The attack catalog

一个。 File & repo based · prompt injection

The attacker puts the payload in a file your coding agent will read.

  • Malicious Markdown / README / AGENTS.md — hidden instructions in a .md file (often in a repo or ~/Downloads) get read by Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor and executed as instructions. The vector most people met first.
  • Rules File Backdoor (Pillar Security, Mar 2025) — the payload hides in a tool's config (.cursor/rules, Copilot instruction files) using zero-width and bidirectional Unicode characters, invisible in the normal GitHub review UI. Both vendors initially treated it as the user's responsibility; GitHub later added a warning when hidden Unicode is detected in file contents. Pillar reported that the payload could persist across forks.
  • Ghostcommit (OffSeq, 2026) — an instruction hidden inside an image tells a coding agent to read .env and smuggle the secrets into code as numeric constants, evading secret scanners because AI reviewers don't inspect image files. (2026 research demonstration.)
🎯 Targets: Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Codex — any agent that reads project files as context.

B. The MCP tool layer · mostly prompt injection

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets agents use external tools. The tools — and their descriptions — are themselves untrusted content.

  • Tool Poisoning (Invariant Labs, Apr 2025) — malicious instructions hidden in a tool's description/metadata, which may not be visible in the client's normal tool presentation but the model reads and obeys. The proof-of-concept made Cursor read ~/.ssh/id_rsa. Now codified as OWASP MCP03:2025.
  • Rug pull — a tool is benign at install, then swaps in malicious behavior in a later update.
  • Tool shadowing — one malicious server redefines or intercepts a trusted server's tool.
  • GitHub MCP exploit (Milanta & Beurer-Kellner, May 2025) — an attacker files a malicious GitHub issue in a public repo; when the agent reads issues, the hidden instruction makes it leak private-repo names into a public pull request. A textbook lethal trifecta.

⚠️ Not prompt injection — an implementation bug: CVE-2025-6514 is an OS command-injection flaw in the mcp-remote OAuth proxy (versions 0.0.5–0.1.15, fixed in 0.1.16, CVSS 9.6). A malicious MCP server a user connects to can run commands on their machine. It's a serious MCP-ecosystem risk, but it has nothing to do with a model obeying a prompt. One academic study reported tool-poisoning indicators in ~5.5% of the open-source MCP servers it sampled — that's a research finding on one sample, not proof that 5.5% of all public servers are exploitable.

C. Invisible text: Unicode, emoji & ANSI smuggling · delivery mechanism

Not an attack on its own — a way to make the instruction invisible to humans while machines still read it.

  • ASCII / Unicode-Tag smuggling — characters in the Unicode Tags block (mainly U+E0020–U+E007E, which mirror printable ASCII) render blank in most contexts but remain readable to the model. Rides in docs, support tickets, web pages, and RAG inputs. Visibility depends on the app. (SecureLayer7, Promptfoo)
  • Emoji smuggling (FireTail, Jan 2026) — instructions hidden inside emoji via variation selectors. In the reported test, the model did not decode them automatically; the researchers had to prompt it to inspect and translate the hidden content. Treat it as a demonstrated technique under specific conditions, not a universal capability.
  • ANSI terminal escape codes (Trail of Bits, Apr 2025) — escape sequences make text invisible in a terminal while the bytes an agent's tool wrapper captures stay intact. Demonstrated against Claude Code; any CLI agent that doesn't strip escapes is exposed.
🧪 Why it's nasty: these characters can sail through human code review and the PR UI — the payload is right there in the diff, you just can't see it.

D . Zero-click via email, calendar & connectors · prompt injection

The scariest class: no click, no download, no action from the victim. The content arrives in a channel the agent automatically ingests.

  • EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711, Aim Labs) — a crafted email sits in the mailbox; when the user later asks Copilot an unrelated question, the email is RAG-pulled into context and exfiltrates SharePoint content, chat history, and files via an auto-fetched Markdown image. Microsoft rated it critical (CVSS 9.3; some trackers score it lower), named the class "LLM Scope Violation," patched it before public disclosure, and reported no known exploitation in the wild.
  • ShadowLeak (Radware) — a service-side injection against ChatGPT's Deep Research agent that exfiltrates Gmail/Drive/Outlook data entirely inside OpenAI's infrastructure, so client-side defenses never see it. Reported to OpenAI in June 2025, fixed by early August, publicly disclosed September 18, 2025.
  • AgentFlayer (Zenity Labs, Aug 2025) — zero-click against ChatGPT Connectors. The demonstrated case hid a prompt in a shared document as nearly invisible white text in a tiny font, told ChatGPT to pull Google Drive secrets, and exfiltrated them through a Markdown image URL. When OpenAI blocked arbitrary image servers, the researchers routed the image through trusted Azure Blob storage. The ChatGPT case was patched; the researchers note other connector targets were flagged "won't fix."
  • "Invitation Is All You Need" (Black Hat, Aug 2025) — promptware hidden in a Google Calendar invite hijacks Gemini when it summarizes your week. Across 14 attack scenarios, researchers rated 73% of the assessed threats high- or critical-risk, including controlled demos of opening smart-home windows and starting calls. Google deployed mitigations. These were controlled research demonstrations, not a real-world campaign in anyone's home.

和。 Browser agents · prompt injection

An AI browser reads every page you visit — including the attacker's. Two separate pieces of research, with different status:

  • Comet page-injection (Brave, Aug 2025) — hidden instructions on a web page executed by the agent as commands, later extended to text hidden in an image. Perplexity shipped initial fixes, but Brave's follow-up testing found the mitigation incomplete. (Simon Willison)
  • CometJacking (LayerX) — a separate crafted-URL attack: opening the link makes the browser's AI run hidden instructions and exfiltrate data. Opening the URL requires user interaction, so this is not zero-click. Per the disclosure, Perplexity marked the report "Not Applicable," and no fix is confirmed in the cited material.
🌐 Browser agents assemble the full trifecta by default: your logged-in sessions, arbitrary web pages, and navigation. Handle with care.

F。 Multimodal & image injection · prompt injection

If the model can read images, the image can carry the payload.

  • Off-white text / "blank" images (Goodside & Rehberger, 2023 →) — subtle text in an apparently blank image can override or bias the model's response. Separately, Rehberger demonstrated an image-borne payload that pushed a model to leak conversation context — exfiltration is a distinct outcome shown in that specific demo. (Simon Willison)
  • Adversarial / visual prompt injection on web agents (2025 research — e.g. VPI-Bench, WebInject) — perturbations and rendered text steer screenshot-driven agents into the wrong action. These are benchmark/lab findings, not disclosed product CVEs.

G。 Supply chain: poisoned models & packages · supply-chain compromise

The compromise ships before any prompt is written. Three distinct incidents often wrongly bundled together:

  • 2024 — ~100 malicious models (JFrog / The Hacker News): pickle-based model files that run arbitrary shell on torch.load().
  • 2025 — PickleScan evasion (PointGuard AI): the nullifAI technique packed malformed pickle files in 7z to slip past Hugging Face's scanner; HF then updated PickleScan.
  • 2026 — fake "OpenAI" repository (InfoWorld): used a malicious loader.py to fetch and run an infostealer (not a torch.load() pickle attack). Reported at 200,000+ downloads (some coverage says 244,000) — but downloads are not confirmed infections, so read that number as reach, not victims.
  • Slopsquatting vs typosquatting — slopsquatting registers package names an LLM hallucinated in generated code; typosquatting mimics real names. A study found hallucinated package names in both commercial and open-source model output. An agent doesn't always auto-install them — but a confident wrong name is a pre-seeded foothold.
🧷 Prefer safetensors over pickle. It removes the unsafe-deserialization risk — but it does not make a malicious repo, loader script, or surrounding package safe.

H. Self-propagating worms · prompt injection, weaponized

  • Morris II (Cohen, Bitton & Nassi, Mar 2024) — the first self-replicating GenAI worm. An adversarial self-replicating prompt lives in a RAG store, performs a malicious action in each app it reaches (spam, data exfiltration), and spreads to the next. Demonstrated against GPT-4, Gemini Pro, and LLaVA in a controlled lab — not released in the wild, but proof that injection + RAG persistence = propagation.

7. Why this is genuinely hard to fix

  • Structure isn't a security boundary. Message roles and formatting exist, but they don't reliably separate trusted instructions from attacker-controlled content. The model infers what to obey from meaning — and meaning is what an attacker controls.
  • Filtering is whack-a-mole. Strip Unicode tag characters and attackers move to emoji variation selectors or rewording. A classifier that catches the obvious attack often misses the reworded one.
  • The capability is the vulnerability. The whole point of an agent is to read untrusted content and take actions. Remove either and you've removed the product.
  • The durable fixes live outside the model — provenance, least privilege, and egress control, enforced whether or not the text fooled the model.

8. What actually helps

No single control solves prompt injection. Defense-in-depth measurably shrinks the blast radius.

Layer 它的作用 Caveat
Break the trifecta Don't give one agent unrestricted private data + untrusted content + outbound actions together The single highest-leverage move
Input sanitization Visualize/escape suspicious characters (Unicode tags, zero-width, ANSI), normalize Does not solve injection — attackers reword or re-encode
Provenance / taint tracking Track where each value came from; treat tool/web output as untrusted Needs enforcement at the action boundary
Least privilege + human-in-the-loop Scope credentials; review sensitive actions Approval only works if the reviewer sees the real action and its arguments
Controlled egress A narrow egress broker, restrict auto-fetching of external images/URLs A broad cloud-domain allowlist is abusable — AgentFlayer used trusted Azure Blob
Output scanning Flag secrets / exfil patterns in output One layer only — data can leave via tool calls, URLs, or images without appearing in the visible reply
Supply-chain hygiene Prefer safetensors; scan models; pin & verify packages safetensors fixes deserialization, not a malicious repo/loader
Secure logging Log raw input to catch hidden code points Redact/escape — raw logs can themselves become a secret store

The highest-leverage idea is the first one, stated carefully:

Avoid giving a single agent unrestricted access to private data, arbitrary untrusted content, and unrestricted outbound actions at once. Where those capabilities are all needed, enforce scoped credentials, tool-level authorization, reviewed sensitive actions, and controlled egress — outside the model.

Design so that when (not if) a hidden instruction gets through, it hits a wall: no private data in reach, or no channel out, or no standing permission to act.

9. A 10-minute checklist

  • [ ] Visualize/escape invisible characters (Unicode tags, zero-width, ANSI) in anything an agent ingests — and treat all external content as untrusted.
  • [ ] Turn off "always allow." Require approval before an agent reads private repos, sends email, moves money, or deletes — and make the prompt show the real destination/arguments.
  • [ ] Use a narrow egress policy — restrict outbound URLs and auto-fetched image hosts; don't trust broad cloud domains wholesale.
  • [ ] Audit your MCP servers — pin versions (update mcp-remote ≥ 0.1.16), read tool descriptions, drop ones you can't vouch for.
  • [ ] Separate the trifecta — don't let one agent session hold private data and untrusted content and an exfil path.
  • [ ] Prefer safetensors; scan models; verify repositories and loader scripts, not just weights.
  • [ ] Log raw input securely (redacted, access-controlled) so hidden code points are reviewable without creating a secret store.
  • [ ] Treat tool and web output as untrusted by default — it's data, never instructions.

10. 外卖

The markdown-file trick that's been making the rounds isn't a one-off — it's one entry in a fast-growing catalog spanning files, tools, invisible text, email, calendars, browsers, images, model weights, and self-replicating worms. The true prompt-injection cases all rhyme because they exploit the same thing: an AI agent can't reliably tell the content it reads from the commands it's given. The rest — implementation bugs and supply-chain compromises — ride in the same systems but need their own fixes.

You don't solve injection with a cleverer prompt. You contain it by designing so that a hidden instruction, when it lands, has nowhere to go. Break the trifecta, enforce authority outside the model, and most of this guide becomes a list of attacks with no payoff.
